card.label: Countersubject
card.learning_takeaway: Identify recurring counterpoint accompanying successive subject entries.
card.card: A countersubject is recurring counterpoint that accompanies a fugue's subject. Its identity matters: the composer brings back recognizable accompanying material when the subject returns, rather than inventing completely different counterpoint each time. The same countersubject can appear in different voices as the texture changes.

evidence.note: Fugue Analysis defines consistent accompaniment and identifies one countersubject in alto and soprano; no requirement that every fugue have one is imposed.

relations.note: The source defines countersubject specifically within its fugue analysis and contrasts it with nonrecurring accompaniment.

card.label: Absolute sensory threshold
card.learning_takeaway: Interpret detection threshold as a probability under controlled conditions.
card.card: An absolute sensory threshold is usually defined as the stimulus intensity detected on half of repeated presentations under specified conditions. It is therefore a probabilistic measurement, not a magical boundary below which detection never happens. The testing conditions matter when comparing how sensitive different observers appear.

evidence.note: OpenStax 5.1 supplies the fifty-percent criterion and controlled conditions; probabilistic interpretation follows that definition without importing unsupported exact sensitivity estimates.
Provides the decision-theoretic premise for the editorial comparison.

relations.note: A detection percentage alone does not separate available sensory information from a decision criterion; signal detection theory analyzes that distinction.

card.label: Stretch tuning
card.learning_takeaway: Explain slightly widened piano octaves through the inharmonicity of stiff strings.
card.card: Piano octaves are often tuned slightly wider than a strict two-to-one frequency ratio. Stiff strings have upper partials sharper than ideal harmonics. Matching the upper note to a lower string's second partial can reduce audible beating, making a mathematically exact octave a poor practical match.

evidence.note: UNSW FAQ gives stretched second partials and beat-eliminating tuning; often and can avoid prescribing one exact stretch for every piano or register.

relations.note: The FAQ explicitly explains stretched tuning as a response to stiffness-induced inharmonicity in struck piano strings.

card.label: Signal detection theory
card.learning_takeaway: Explore detecting a target among noise when expectations and task goals influence reports.
card.card: Signal detection theory separates sensory evidence from the criterion for reporting a signal. With evidence quality held fixed, lowering the criterion can increase both hits and false alarms; raising it can reduce both. Better sensitivity and greater willingness to answer yes are different changes.

evidence.note: Heeger’s Information and Criterion discussion and Figures 2–4 distinguish changing a criterion along one ROC from changing evidence quality. The revised card explicitly holds information fixed for the criterion tradeoff and makes no clinical recommendation.
Separates information quality and decision criterion, and shows the hit/false-alarm tradeoff.

relations.note: A fifty-percent detection threshold summarizes responses, while signal detection theory distinguishes evidence quality from the criterion behind those responses.

card.label: Mixed-member proportional representation
card.learning_takeaway: See how constituency representation combines with a party-proportional seat total.
card.card: Mixed-member proportional representation combines constituency representatives with party-list seats intended to make overall representation proportional. In New Zealand's version, voters choose a local candidate and a party separately. The party vote largely determines each party's total seats, while electorate winners take individual constituency seats.

evidence.locator: Two votes; electorate MPs and list MPs
evidence.note: New Zealand Electoral Commission's MMP explanation supports separate votes and the overall party share; intended and largely accommodate allocation qualifications, and New Zealand's version prevents universalizing its exact rules.

relations.note: The official MMP explanation identifies the threshold as the New Zealand eligibility rule operating within this electoral system, not as a universal property of MMP.

card.label: Milgram's obedience experiments
card.learning_takeaway: Compare obedience in the original setup with changes produced by proximity and setting.
card.card: Milgram's participants believed they were administering increasingly strong shocks when an experimenter instructed them to continue; the learner actually received none. In the original setting, many continued to the highest level. Changing the setting or bringing the learner closer reduced obedience, limiting any simple universal conclusion.

evidence.note: Section 12.4 describes the deceptive shock setup and lower continuation rates in office/proximity variants; no claim that all participants obeyed or that this settles explanations of historical atrocities.

relations.note: Milgram tests responses to an experimenter's commands, whereas Asch tests responses to a group's judgments. The comparison distinguishes authority-directed obedience from peer conformity.

card.label: Seki
card.learning_takeaway: Recognize mutual survival when either attack would allow the opponent to capture.
card.card: Seki is mutual survival in Go without each group having two independent eyes. Neighboring groups share a shortage of liberties, and either player's attempt to capture can allow the opponent to capture first. Leaving the position alone therefore preserves both sides' stones.

evidence.locator: Seki: a kind of local stalemate
evidence.note: BGA's seki examples support mutual stand-off and shortage of liberties; no universal territory-scoring rule is added because rulesets differ.

relations.note: The guide introduces seki as an exception to the simple expectation that a group lacking two eyes will die.

card.label: Bach's Fugue in C minor, BWV 847
card.learning_takeaway: Trace full subject entries alternating with development through fragmented motives.
card.card: Bach's C-minor fugue from the first Well-Tempered Clavier offers a compact lesson in contrapuntal development. Its opening exposition introduces the subject in every voice. Episodes then work with smaller fragments of subjects and countersubjects, allowing recognizable material to generate passages without a complete subject statement.

evidence.note: The detailed analysis identifies first exposition, all-voice entries and fragmented material in episodes; no unsupported numerical count of voices or episodes is added.

relations.note: The source explicitly analyzes BWV 847 as a fugue with expositions and episodes.

card.label: Two truths in Indian Buddhist philosophy
card.learning_takeaway: Distinguish conventional and ultimate truth while recognizing that Buddhist schools interpret the distinction differently.
card.card: Indian Buddhist discussions of two truths distinguish conventional understanding from an ultimate perspective. Ordinary language and practices operate conventionally, while ultimate analysis asks how things really are. Buddhist schools interpret both levels and their relationship differently, so the distinction does not express one uniform doctrine across traditions.

evidence.note: SEP opening differentiates conventional and ultimate perspectives and explicitly warns that the schools can be radically opposed; the card avoids attributing one settled metaphysics or historical origin to all Buddhism.

relations.note: The distinction concerns perspectives on truth and knowledge, inviting comparison with epistemology's study of cognitive success without assimilating all Buddhist schools to a single Western theory.

card.label: Mode locking in bowed strings
card.learning_takeaway: See how periodic bowing can enforce harmonic motion despite inharmonic string resonances.
card.card: A bow alternately sticks to and slips against a string, sustaining a nearly periodic motion. That nonlinear drive can pull the string's slightly mismatched resonances into harmonic frequency ratios. The resulting steady note can therefore be more harmonically regular than the freely vibrating string's natural modes.

evidence.note: UNSW explicitly attributes harmonic locking to periodic stick-slip drive; can and steady note preserve its operating-condition qualification.

relations.note: The source explains mode locking as the reason bowed motion can be harmonic despite slightly inharmonic natural resonances.

card.label: Just intonation
card.learning_takeaway: Explore why pure small-ratio intervals create compromises when changing keys.
card.card: Just intonation favors intervals described by simple frequency ratios. Yet pure fifths and pure thirds do not fit every chain of notes identically: repeated three-to-two fifths can conflict with a pure third. Fixed-pitch instruments must therefore confront compromises that adjustable voices or strings can handle differently.

evidence.locator: What is all the fuss about temperament?
evidence.note: UNSW temperament discussion supplies the chain-of-fifths mismatch and fixed versus adjustable instrument distinction; no claim that one tuning is universally best.

relations.note: The FAQ directly contrasts just intonation with meantone's compromise between thirds and fifths.

card.label: Fake-barn case
card.learning_takeaway: Explore how a deceptive environment can undermine otherwise accurate perception.
card.card: In the fake-barn case, Henry happens to see a real barn in a landscape full of convincing facades. His belief is true and apparently justified, yet could easily have been mistaken. The example challenges whether accurate perception alone guarantees knowledge in a systematically deceptive environment.

evidence.note: SEP section 4's Barn County passage supplies Henry, the real barn and facades; apparently and challenges preserve the evaluative character of the knowledge verdict.

relations.note: The source presents Barn County as a challenge to the no-false-lemmas repair because Henry's belief need not involve inference from a false premise.

card.label: Bearing off in backgammon
card.learning_takeaway: Explore the conditions for removing checkers and using an oversized die roll.
card.card: Bearing off removes checkers from a backgammon board, but only after all your active checkers reach your home board. A roll normally removes a checker from its matching point. An oversized roll can remove the highest remaining checker when no checker occupies a higher point.

evidence.note: USBGF Bearing Off supplies prerequisites and oversized-roll rule; wording avoids requiring removal when another legal move is possible.

relations.note: Bearing off is explicitly the final removal process that completes backgammon's race.

card.label: Jacoby rule
card.learning_takeaway: See how an optional scoring rule encourages use of the doubling cube.
card.card: The optional Jacoby rule makes a gammon or backgammon count as a single game unless a double has been offered. It encourages use of the cube rather than waiting for a multiple-value win. The cited standard match-play rules do not use it.

evidence.locator: Optional Rules: Jacoby Rule; FAQ on match play
evidence.note: USBGF Optional Rules gives the condition and incentive; its match-play FAQ explicitly excludes Jacoby. The card preserves that format boundary instead of treating the optional convention as universal.

relations.note: The source explains Jacoby's purpose through whether players use the doubling cube during the game.

card.label: Money bills under the Parliament Acts
card.learning_takeaway: Compare the Lords' restricted role over money bills with other public bills.
card.card: Under the UK Parliament Acts, a Speaker-certified money bill can reach Royal Assent without Lords consent after a month without unamended passage. It must already have passed the Commons and reached the Lords at least a month before session-end; the Commons can direct otherwise.

evidence.locator: Bills subject to the Parliament Acts
evidence.note: The Parliamentary Counsel guidance, paragraphs 1.2, 1.5, 1.8 and 2.2, supplies certification and all timing/direction conditions; this supersedes the introductory page's misleading claim of automatic assent within a month and its absolute amendment claim.

evidence.locator: Paragraphs 1.2, 1.5, 1.8 and 2.2; 2.7 and 2.19 resolve misleading simplifications
evidence.note: Official guidance supports certification, Commons passage, session timing, a month without unamended Lords passage, Commons contrary direction and Royal Assent; not automatic enactment after a month.

relations.note: The guidance expressly identifies section 1 of the 1911 Act as the money-bill procedure and reproduces its legal conditions.

card.label: Meantone temperament
card.learning_takeaway: See how slightly narrowed fifths improve thirds but constrain modulation.
card.card: Meantone temperament narrows fifths to improve the tuning of major thirds. The discrepancy is distributed across a chain of fifths rather than left entirely in the resulting third. This can suit particular keys well, while movement into other keys exposes the compromise's limits.

evidence.locator: What is all the fuss about temperament?
evidence.note: UNSW's worked example describes thirds improved by narrowing four fifths and worsening problems in other keys; no relation is made to personality temperament Q80157.

relations.note: The cited tuning comparison presents meantone as a different way to reconcile pure-interval demands on fixed-pitch instruments.

card.label: Misinformation effect
card.learning_takeaway: Explore how misleading information after an event can alter later reports.
card.card: Later information can alter how an earlier event is remembered. In Loftus and Palmer's car-crash studies, wording in questions affected speed estimates and later reports of broken glass. The finding shows how post-event suggestions can shape reports, rather than proving that every eyewitness memory is inaccurate.

evidence.note: OpenStax describes both question wording and later glass reports; studies plural avoids treating the different experimental stages as one undifferentiated sample.

relations.note: These are different routes to memory distortion: external post-event suggestion versus confusion over a detail's source.

card.label: Neapolitan chord
card.learning_takeaway: Recognize the flattened-supertonic major chord as a chromatic predominant.
card.card: The Neapolitan chord is a major chord built on the lowered second scale degree. In classical tonal analysis it commonly appears in first inversion and serves a predominant function. Its distinctive chromatic color therefore has a directional role, helping prepare the approach to dominant harmony.

evidence.note: Section 20.1 names flat II, most-common first inversion and predominant function; major quality follows the uppercase chord notation, not a claim that every flat-II sonority has this function.

relations.note: The Neapolitan's predominant role contrasts with the cadential six-four's dominant role, despite both often occurring near a cadence.

card.label: Sensory adaptation
card.learning_takeaway: Distinguish continuing sensory stimulation from reduced conscious notice over time.
card.card: With prolonged stimulation, a continuing sensory input can become less noticeable even while it remains present. OpenStax describes this as sensory adaptation. The change highlights a gap between continuing stimulation and conscious experience, helping explain why an initially prominent feature of the surroundings can fade from awareness.

evidence.note: OpenStax's perception section explicitly describes reduced notice during continued stimulation; this phenomenological card does not assert a particular receptor mechanism or equate every attention lapse with adaptation.

relations.note: Reduced notice of sustained input differs from missing a visible unexpected event while concentrating on another task.

card.label: Pedal point
card.learning_takeaway: Hear a held note change harmonic status while surrounding chords move.
card.card: A pedal point holds one note while surrounding harmonies change. It begins as a chord tone but can become a non-chord tone against later chords. Often heard in the bass, it can also appear higher up, creating continuity while its harmonic meaning shifts.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 10.8 supports changing harmonic status, frequent bass placement and upper-voice pedals; the card does not restrict the device to a literal organ pedal.

relations.note: Both can sustain a note across a harmonic change, but the pedal persists across harmonies while a suspension has a prepared stepwise resolution.

card.label: Two Pages
card.learning_takeaway: Explore Glass's additive process through repetitions that successively omit final notes.
card.card: At the opening of Philip Glass's Two Pages, growth comes from adding repetitions whose final notes are progressively removed. A motive can therefore expand while newly added units become shorter. The cited analysis illustrates how repetition and subtraction can cooperate within an additive process.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 35.1 explicitly limits its Two Pages demonstration to the opening and labels the notation a transcription/analysis. The card does not assert that every section of the entire work follows the displayed process.

relations.note: The textbook analyzes the opening of Glass's Two Pages as an example of additive process, with shortening repetitions inside the expanding unit.

card.label: Figure–ground (perception)
card.learning_takeaway: See why a single image can reverse between an object and its background.
card.card: Figure–ground organization separates a focal object from its background. In the familiar vase-and-faces image, the same boundary can outline a white vase or two dark faces. Changing which region counts as the figure changes what the image seems to depict.
card.original_description: humans' ability to separate foreground from background in visual images

evidence.note: Section 5.6, figure-ground paragraph and Figure 5.25, support segmentation and the reversible vase/faces example; the card avoids claiming that segmentation must always precede recognition.

relations.note: Compare selecting an object against its background with perceptually completing an incomplete object; these are distinct operations illustrated in the same Gestalt discussion.

imported_records.description: humans' ability to separate foreground from background in visual images

sample.selection_reason: Purposive coverage/risk selection: risk:editorial_relationship, risk:fine_application_wording, risk:qualification_or_assumption

card.label: Knuckleball aerodynamics
card.learning_takeaway: Understand erratic flight from seam-dependent forces varying during the pitch.
card.card: A baseball's seams make its surface aerodynamically uneven. As their orientation changes during flight, the effective location and direction of aerodynamic forces can vary. NASA connects these unsteady forces with the knuckleball's erratic motion, rather than explaining it solely through a steady spin-generated curve.

evidence.locator: Lift: stitches and center of pressure
evidence.note: NASA Forces on a Baseball, Lift, supports seam-dependent pressure changes and erratic motion; contrast with its separate simplified curveball model is labeled editorial in the relationship.
Steady spinning-ball trajectory is a comparison premise, not the knuckleball explanation itself.

relations.note: Contrasting seam-sensitive, time-varying forces with a regular spinning-ball model separates two different explanations of curved baseball flight.

card.label: Political science
card.learning_takeaway: Examine how rules and participants' choices shape collective decisions involving government.
card.card: Political science examines collective choices and conflicts, especially those involving government. A useful analysis asks which rules apply, what circumstances participants face and what choices they make. The same formal rule can produce different outcomes when the surrounding conditions or participants' strategies change.

evidence.note: OpenStax section 1.1 defines government-focused collective interactions and the rules/reality/choices framework; the final sentence expresses their interaction rather than a quantified causal finding.

relations.note: The chapter identifies a constitution as the most basic legal rules structuring government, one important instance of the rules its political-analysis framework examines.

imported_records.subsection: Society and social sciences / Politics / Political science and the state

sample.selection_reason: Purposive coverage/risk selection: risk:fine_application_wording, risk:qualification_or_assumption, risk:source_asserted_relationship

card.label: No-false-lemmas condition
card.learning_takeaway: Evaluate the proposed repair that knowledge cannot be inferred from false premises.
card.card: The no-false-lemmas condition proposes repairing justified true belief by excluding beliefs inferred from false premises. It blocks some Gettier examples, but deceptive perceptual environments pose a further challenge. A belief can apparently be accidentally true without having been inferred from any false proposition.

evidence.note: SEP section 4 states the proposed fourth condition and noninferential counterexamples; the card does not claim the repair is accepted or sufficient.

relations.note: The entry expressly develops no false lemmas as an attempted additional condition for solving the Gettier problem, then presents objections.

card.label: Henry Molaison
card.learning_takeaway: Compare impaired new declarative memories with preserved improvement on practiced tasks.
card.card: Henry Molaison, known in research as H. M., had severe difficulty forming new declarative memories after brain surgery. Yet he could improve at repeatedly practiced tasks without remembering previous practice. His case separates conscious memory for an episode from learning expressed through better performance.

evidence.note: PubMed abstract of Augustinack et al. directly identifies Henry Molaison as H. M.; OpenStax 8.2 supports surgery and declarative impairment, and 8.3 supports improved performance without recalled practice. Do not claim all old memories remained intact.
Identifies H. M. and the effect of his operation on declarative memory; does not supply his full name.
Directly identifies Henry Molaison as H. M. and describes the operation causing his amnesia.

relations.note: The textbook explicitly uses H. M. to contrast impaired new episodic/semantic memory with preserved procedural learning.

card.label: Issue preclusion
card.learning_takeaway: Distinguish relitigating a decided issue from repeating an entire claim.
card.card: In US litigation, issue preclusion bars repeating a factual or legal issue already validly, finally and necessarily decided in an earlier proceeding. It can matter even when a later lawsuit is a different claim. The focus is the resolved issue, rather than repetition of the original action.

evidence.note: Cornell's collateral-estoppel definition and civil-procedure discussion support final and necessary determination; can matter avoids promising automatic preclusion without the jurisdiction's additional requirements.
The claim-level definition supports the stated contrast with a previously decided issue.

relations.note: The linked accounts distinguish preventing a repeated claim from preventing a repeated decision on an essential issue, while acknowledging varied uses of the term res judicata.

card.label: Pitch (music)
card.learning_takeaway: Relate perceived high and low notes to their ordering on a keyboard.
card.card: Pitch is a sound's perceived highness or lowness. On a piano, moving right produces higher notes. For periodic musical tones, doubling the vibration frequency raises pitch by an octave, showing why musical intervals depend on frequency ratios rather than equal additions of hertz.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 1.1 supports keyboard direction; UNSW's pitch discussion supplies periodic-tone frequency and octave ratio. Keep this auditory meaning separate from material pitch.

evidence.locator: Pitch, frequency, harmonics and missing fundamental
evidence.note: Frequency ratios, including doubling for an octave, support the quantitative explanation.

relations.note: The UNSW pitch discussion explicitly uses a missing fundamental to show that perceived pitch can persist when the lowest-frequency component is absent.

card.label: Komi
card.learning_takeaway: Understand points compensating White for playing second.
card.card: Komi compensates the player using White stones for Black's first move in Go. It adds points to White's final score rather than adding stones to the board. The British Go Association's cited default uses seven-and-a-half points; other rules or agreements can use different values.

evidence.note: BGA Default Rules gives 7½ and contrasts traditional Japanese values; How to Play explains compensation rather than placement of stones.
The guide explains compensation to White for Black moving first.

relations.note: The tournament rules identify komi as a score adjustment within Go, separately from handicap-stone placement.

card.label: Appoggiatura
card.learning_takeaway: Follow an expressive non-chord note approached by leap and resolved by step.
card.card: An appoggiatura is a non-chord tone approached by a leap and left by a step. It is usually accented, placing the dissonance on a strong moment before resolution. The resolving step can go upward or downward; the expressive effect does not require one fixed direction.

evidence.note: Puget Sound 10.4 supports leap approach, step departure, usual accent and either resolution direction; maintain its analytical sense rather than every historical ornamental use of the term.
The prepared same-note approach of a suspension supports the editorial contrast.

relations.note: Both can create accented non-chord tension, but an appoggiatura arrives by leap whereas a suspension is prepared by the same note.

card.label: Shogi
card.learning_takeaway: Explain the piece-reuse feature of shogi through a directly supported broad-game overview, leaving the perpetual-check exception to its separate rule card.
card.card: Shogi is Japanese chess with a distinctive form of piece reuse. Captured pieces become reserves for their captor. Instead of moving a piece already on the board, a player can spend a turn returning a captured piece to play on their own side.
card.original_description: Exploring Japanese chess and its distinctive piece-reuse strategies.

evidence.locator: PDF pages 1, 3 and 12, Comparisons and Placing Captured Pieces
evidence.note: Captured pieces become the captor’s reserves and may be returned to play instead of moving a board piece; no unrestricted-drop or automatic-promotion claim is used.

relations.note: The guide explicitly compares shogi with European chess and identifies returning captured pieces as a difference.

imported_records.description: Exploring Japanese chess and its distinctive piece-reuse strategies.

card.label: Othello
card.learning_takeaway: Understand how a placement changes ownership of intervening discs.
card.card: Othello changes the ownership of pieces already on the board. A player places a disc to bracket an uninterrupted line of opposing discs, then flips those discs to their color. The winner has more discs when neither player can make a legal move.

evidence.note: Official outflanking and ending rules support placement, flipping and the final majority; the game need not fill all sixty-four squares.

relations.note: A lack of outflanking moves determines both forced passes and the eventual end of the game.

card.label: Chess
card.learning_takeaway: Understand why checkmate ends play without capturing the king.
card.card: Chess ends in checkmate when the opposing king is attacked and no legal move can remove the threat. The king is never actually captured. A different ending, stalemate, occurs when a player has no legal move but their king is not attacked.
card.original_description: Exploring strategic play, tactics and positional thinking in chess.

evidence.note: Articles 1.4 and 5.2.1 support the objective, prohibition of king capture and contrasting stalemate condition; no claim that every immobile king is stalemated.

relations.note: The laws distinguish checkmate from stalemate through whether the immobile side's king is attacked.

imported_records.description: Exploring strategic play, tactics and positional thinking in chess.

card.label: Bach's Invention in C major, BWV 772
card.learning_takeaway: Recognize inversion and rhythmic augmentation within one tightly developed keyboard work.
card.card: Bach's C-major Invention shows how a short idea can sustain development. The opening notes return with their melodic direction inverted, and fragments also appear in rhythmic augmentation. These transformations preserve recognizable material while changing its contour or the amount of time it occupies.

evidence.note: Section 11.2 identifies the first seven notes inverted later and an augmented fragment; the wording does not claim every occurrence transforms the whole theme.

relations.note: The textbook explicitly labels the invention's returning opening notes as melodic inversion.

card.label: Stratified sortition for citizens’ assemblies
card.learning_takeaway: See how lottery recruitment and demographic stratification produce an intended mini-public.
card.card: Ireland's citizens' assembly recruitment combines chance with demographic balancing. Randomly invited households may nominate an adult applicant; members are then selected using demographic information so the group broadly resembles society. The resulting mini-public is intended to be diverse, rather than simply comprising whoever volunteers first.

evidence.locator: How are members selected?; recruitment method
evidence.note: The official FAQ's recruitment paragraphs describe random household invitations, one adult nominee and stratified selection among applicants; intended and broadly avoid claiming perfect representativeness or eliminating nonresponse effects.

relations.note: The source explicitly identifies stratified selection as the membership-recruitment procedure for Irish citizens' assemblies, connecting mechanism and deliberative body.

card.label: Tennis racket sweet spot
card.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a low-vibration impact location from the point of maximum rebound speed.
card.card: Physicist Rod Cross distinguishes a tennis racket's vibration-node sweet spot from its center of percussion and point of fastest rebound. An impact at the vibration node removes that component of handle motion, but rotation and translation can still transmit forces to the hand.

evidence.note: Cross sections 1 and 3 expressly separate the vibration node, center of percussion and maximum rebound, with rotation/translation/vibration components. Attribution avoids treating one terminology choice as the only sense of sweet spot.

relations.note: The source directly compares a vibration-node sweet spot with the separate center-of-percussion concept.

card.label: Circumstantial moral luck
card.learning_takeaway: Ask how unchosen situations expose people to different moral tests.
card.card: Circumstantial moral luck concerns the unchosen situations that test a person's character. Someone placed in a brutal political environment may face choices another person never encounters. The philosophical problem is whether differing moral assessments are justified when the opportunity for wrongdoing itself depended on luck.

evidence.note: SEP's circumstantial-luck paragraph compares collaborators with imagined counterparts elsewhere; the card generalizes that structure without excusing atrocities or asserting that circumstances compel every action.

relations.note: Nagel's taxonomy in the entry expressly treats luck in one's circumstances as a kind of moral luck affecting assessment.

card.label: Perpetual check in shogi
card.learning_takeaway: Compare ordinary repetition with repeated checks that make the checking player lose.
card.card: Repeated checking is not a safe route to a draw in shogi. Under the Japan Shogi Association's cited explanation, if continuous checks produce the same position four times, the player giving those checks loses. Ordinary repetition without continuous checking is treated differently.

evidence.locator: 連続王手の千日手というのは反則なのですか
evidence.note: The official Japanese FAQ supports the fourth-occurrence loss and distinguishes ordinary repetition; the broad Shogi card instead explains piece reuse.

relations.note: The Japan Shogi Association identifies this as shogi's special treatment of repetition by continuous check.

card.label: FOIA segregability
card.learning_takeaway: See why an exempt passage need not justify withholding the entire record.
card.card: FOIA segregability means an exempt passage does not necessarily justify withholding an entire record. Federal agencies must consider partial disclosure and release reasonably separable nonexempt portions after redaction. The practical question is what can still be disclosed without revealing the information protected by a valid exemption.

evidence.note: 5 USC 552(a)(8)(A)(ii) and the final paragraph of (b) require reasonable segregation and partial release; reasonably and valid exemption preserve limits rather than promising every document has releasable fragments.

relations.note: The statute itself imposes partial-disclosure and segregation duties within FOIA, tying the mechanism directly to the federal records-access regime.

card.label: Research debriefing
card.learning_takeaway: Understand why concealed research purposes must be explained after deceptive studies.
card.card: Research debriefing explains a study after participation, especially when its purpose was concealed. Participants receive an honest account of the research question, the use of their data and why deception was used. The explanation helps restore information that the study deliberately withheld during the task.

evidence.note: Section 2.4 explicitly requires a full explanation after deceptive studies, including purpose, data use, reasons and further information; the card does not promise that explanation erases any harm.

relations.note: The ethics passage makes debriefing a requirement following deception and specifies the information participants should receive.
